scenes.heading: Analysing and reporting results
scenes.say: Collecting data is only half an investigation. The other half is making sense of it and deciding whether your results can be trusted.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Bathroom scales that always read 2 kg heavy
scenes.science: Systematic error shifts every result the same way
scenes.breaks: in a real experiment you usually don't know the true value, so systematic errors are harder to spot.
scenes.say: Imagine bathroom scales that always read two kilos heavy. Weigh yourself five times and you get almost the same number, so it's precise. But every reading is wrong in the same direction, so it's not accurate. That's a systematic error. More repeats won't fix it. You have to calibrate the scales.
scenes.caption: Imagine bathroom scales that always read 2 kg heavy. Weigh yourself five times and you get almost the same number, so it's precise. But every reading is wrong in the same direction, so it's not accurate. That's a systematic error. More repeats won't fix it. You have to calibrate the scales.

scenes.heading: Accuracy vs precision
scenes.say: Picture a dartboard. Accurate means darts near the bullseye, the true value. Precise means darts tightly grouped together, wherever they land. You can be tightly grouped in the wrong corner: precise but not accurate.

scenes.heading: Two kinds of error
scenes.say: Random scatters, systematic shifts. Random error spreads results either side of the true value, and more repeats help. Systematic error pushes every result the same way, so you need to fix the method or calibrate the equipment.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: A reference sample is 5.00 g. Student P gets 4.70, 4.71, 4.69 g. Student Q gets 5.10, 4.85, 5.05 g.
scenes.say: The true mass is five grams. Student P's results are close together but about point three grams low: precise but not accurate, a systematic error, like an unzeroed balance. Student Q's mean is exactly five, but the results are spread out: accurate but not precise, a random error.

scenes.heading: Graphs
points: DRY MIX: dependent on Y, independent on X
Line of best fit: not dot to dot
scenes.say: For graphs, remember DRY MIX: dependent variable on the Y axis, independent on the X axis. A line of best fit shows the trend, with points spread evenly above and below. Reading inside your data is reliable. Extending beyond it is risky.

scenes.heading: Writing a conclusion
scenes.say: A good conclusion answers the aim and quotes your data. Say whether the hypothesis was supported, never proven. And don't claim anything beyond the range you tested.

points: Accuracy: close to the true value
Conclusions quote data and answer the aim
scenes.say: Quick recap. Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeats. Random errors scatter, systematic errors shift. Conclusions should quote data and answer the aim. Now try the practice questions!
